A novel improved Frilled Lizard algorithm for solving the optimal planning
problem of renewable energy sources within distribution grids under
uncertainties
Badreddine Bendriss a
 ,∗, Samir Sayah a
 , Abdellatif Hamouda b
a QUERE Laboratory, Department of Electrical Engineering, Ferhat Abbas University, Setif 1, Algeria

A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Frilled lizard algorithm
Optimal planning problem
Renewable energy sources
Wind turbine
Solar photovoltaic
A B S T R A C T
In this research, a new improved frilled lizard optimization algorithm is designed and proposed to address the
optimal planning problem of renewable energy sources-based distributed generation within radial distribution
grids. The primary objective is to minimize power losses, elevate the voltage profile, and improve voltage
stability, formulated as a multi-objective optimization problem. The planning process of renewable energy
sources in the radial distribution grid is a complex problem that requires accounting for uncertainties in
renewable energy sources’ power output and load demand fluctuations. To this end, we have developed an
appropriate probability model to estimate the stochastic power generation from renewable energy sources
based on hourly seasonal data, including wind speed, solar irradiance, and ambient temperature collected over
a specified time frame and location. The developed improved frilled lizard optimization technique incorporates
three distinct strategies: fitness distance balance, quasi-opposite-based learning, and Cauchy mutation, to
enhance its searching capabilities and avoid falling into local optimal traps. The suggested improved frilled
lizard optimization is successfully applied to identify the optimal locations and rating capacities of solar
photovoltaic strings and wind turbines, as well as the power factor of wind turbines. The effectiveness of the
presented approach is demonstrated using the IEEE 85-bus distribution grid. To further assess its feasibility
and robustness, a performance comparison is conducted against other recent effective algorithms, including
the grey wolf optimizer, the black-winged kite algorithm, and the original frilled lizard optimization. Results
show that the proposed improved frilled lizard optimization technique significantly reduces annual average
power losses by 70.25%, decreases voltage deviation by 78.51%, and improves the voltage stability index by
20.79%, outperforming other methods.
1. Introduction
Recently, the surge in electricity demand has become increasingly
evident due to economic development and the installation of new
facilities to accommodate the growing population. The traditional re-
sponse to meet this higher demand involves augmenting the power
plant capacities through further combustion. However, this approach is
neither economically effective nor environmentally sound, as it relies
heavily on fossil fuels [1]. Moreover, the rising loads introduce poten-
tial operational issues for the distribution grid, such as increased power
losses, voltage drops, degradation in power quality, and deterioration
in system stability, particularly due to its radial structure. [2,3].
Renewable energy sources (RESs) such as solar photovoltaics (PVs)
systems and wind turbines (WTs) based distributed generations (DGs)

offer an alternative solution to meet the growing demand for electricity
and enhance the performance of radial distribution grids (RDGs). RESs
are cost-effective and environmentally friendly, referring to small-scale
electricity generation, placed near the end-consumers [4,5]. Integrating
RESs into the RDG offers substantial benefits, including, reduced power
losses, improved voltage profile, enhanced system stability, decreased
carbon gas emissions and alleviated heavy loads. However, these bene-
fits cannot be earned until DGs are strategically located and optimally
sized [6]. Improper placement and sizing of DGs can negatively impact
system performance, such as increased power losses, poor voltage pro-
files, system instability, reverse power flow and improper functioning
of protection devices [7,8]. Therefore, effectively integrating RESs into
RDGs presents a crucial challenge for many researchers and engineers.

Nonetheless, the intermittent nature and unpredictability of RESs
introduce additional challenges and intricacies in optimal grid plan-
ning. Wind and solar power generation are particularly affected by
meteorological conditions. WTs depend on wind speed, while PV sys-
tems are influenced by solar irradiance and ambient temperature at a
specific time and a geographic location. These dependencies, coupled
with fluctuations in load demand, complicate the proper incorporation
of RESs into the RDG. Addressing these challenges is a crucial step
toward maximizing the effectiveness of RES integration and ensuring
a reliable and sustainable power system [9].
In the academic literature, many studies have attempted to solve
the optimal planning problem (OPP) of DGs within the RDG, each
considering specific objectives, either as a single or multi-objective
problem formulation. These studies involve the application of different
optimization techniques, encompassing the whale optimization algo-
rithm (WOA) [10], the equilibrium optimizer (EO) algorithm [11],
the improved wild horse optimization (IWHO) algorithm [12] and
the adaptive particle swarm optimization (APSO) [13] to identify the
optimal size and site of DGs for reducing power loss. Also, the coyote
optimization algorithm (COA) [14] has been applied to find the best
site and size of DG units to reduce power loss, lower operating costs,
and improve voltage stability. The modified gravitational search algo-
rithm (MGSA) [15], the artificial bee colony (ABC) algorithm [3] and
the arithmetic optimization algorithm (AOA) [16] have been employed
to identify the best site and location of DG units for reducing power
losses and elevate the voltage profile. Furthermore, the quasi opposi-
tional chaotic symbiotic organisms search (QOCSOS) algorithm [5] and
the grey wolf optimization (GWO) [17] were applied to pinpoint the
optimal size and site of DG units to reduce power loss, improve voltage
profile, and enhance system stability.
Overall, the above studies focused on addressing the DG sizing and
location problem by considering peak load conditions. Additionally,
the uncertainties associated with renewable sources have been omitted.
However, other studies have addressed the integration of renewable
energy sources, considering their intermittent nature and variable load
demands within the distribution grid from various perspectives. For
example Kayal and Chanda [18] focused on optimizing the locations
and capacities of mixed solar and wind energy sources in an Indian
rural 28-bus distribution grid. The weighted aggregation particle swarm
optimization (WAPSO) algorithm was utilized to reduce power losses,
enhance voltage stability, and improve network security while account-
ing for uncertainties in solar irradiance and wind speed. Hemeida
et al. [19], presented a methodology for optimizing DGs placement
in power systems considering load uncertainties. The approach utilizes
Monte Carlo simulation to generate various load scenarios employing
four bio-inspired optimization techniques, namely grey wolf optimiza-
tion (GWO), manta ray foraging optimization (MRFO), satin bowerbird
optimization (SBO), and whale optimization algorithm (WOA). The
objective was to reduce active power loss, voltage deviation, and
maximize the voltage stability index. In [20], the authors suggested
a strategy for allocating PV and battery energy storage systems using
a modified Henry gas solubility optimization (HGSO) algorithm to
minimize total system power loss, considering PV generation uncer-
tainties and time-varying loads. In [21], the authors introduced a novel
approach employing genetic algorithms (GA) to optimize the allocation
of capacitor banks (CB) and distributed PV generation in unbalanced
distribution grids. The method included conducting sensitivity analy-
sis using GA to pinpoint optimal allocation zones where placing PV
and CB could minimize losses. The study customized GA to man-
age uncertainties in load and PV generation over a 24-hour planning
horizon. Khasanov et al. [22], suggested an artificial ecosystem-based
optimization–opposition-based learning (AEO-OBL), to optimize the
placement of PV and WT-based DGs on IEEE 33-bus and 85-bus RDGs.
The improved algorithm incorporates five strategies to enhance the
search capability and achieve a balance between the exploration and
exploitation phases, addressing the stochastic nature of RESs and mak-
ing it effective for minimizing system power losses. In [23], the rider
optimization algorithm (ROA) has been proposed to identify the opti-
mal size and site of RES, specifically WTs, PVs and biomass-based DG
units in standard 33 and 69-bus distribution grids. The study aimed to
minimize total energy losses while considering the fluctuations in wind
speed and solar irradiation. The authors of [24] introduces the artificial
hummingbird algorithm (AHA) for optimal sizing and positions of RESs
in IEEE 33-bus and actual 94-bus RDGs, effectively minimizing costs,
emissions, and voltage deviations while enhancing voltage stability,
considering uncertainties. A pseudo-inspired gravitational search algo-
rithm (PI-GSA) is introduced in [25] as a novel approach to optimize
the allocation and sizing of RERs in IEEE 15-bus, 33-bus and 69-
bus distribution grids. The algorithm considered uncertainties related
to PV and wind output, electricity prices, and load variations using
probability distribution functions. In [26], a hybrid model for integrat-
ing renewable energy sources into the IEEE 33-bus distribution grid
is proposed, using a bi-directional long short-term memory network
to manage uncertainties from PV and wind generation. The model,
optimized with binary particle swarm optimization (BPSO), aimed to
minimize energy losses and voltage deviations while considering long-
term and seasonal impacts. Most of these studies have addressed the
OPP of RESs while considering load, solar irradiation, and wind speed
uncertainties. However, they have largely overlooked temperature-
related uncertainties, which limits their scope. Additional limitations in
the existing literature include the assumption of fixed locations or sizes
for RESs, as well as the neglect of certain grid constraints. Moreover,
the majority of these approaches assumed that WTs operate at unity
power factors (PFs). Consequently, these studies focus exclusively on
the location and size of the WTs, neglecting the optimization of their
PF, which is crucial for enhancing system performance and overall grid
efficiency. Table 1 summarizes the current work and other relevant
research on the OPP of RESs within RDG.
In this paper, we present a novel optimization approach, termed the
Improved Frilled Lizard (IFLO) algorithm, designed to simultaneously
determine the optimal positions and number of WTs and PV strings,
as well as the optimal PF of WTs, within the 85-bus radial distribution
grid. Our primary objective includes minimizing average annual power
losses and voltage deviation (VD) while maximizing the yearly aver-
age voltage stability index (VSI) within operational constraints. The
study considers uncertainties in RES, including fluctuations in wind
speed, availability of solar irradiance, temperature variations, and time-
varying load demand, based on real historical collected data from the
study area over a seasonal planning horizon. The proposed approach is
evaluated against several established optimization techniques, includ-
ing the well-known Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO) [27], Harris Hawks
optimization (HHO) [28], Chernobyl Disaster Optimizer (CDO) [29],
Dingo Optimization Algorithm (DOA) [30], Whale Optimization Algo-
rithm (WOA) [31], Black-winged Kite Algorithm (BKA) [32] and the
original FLO [33]. However, the novelty and main achievements of this
research are summarized below:
1. A novel Improved Frilled Lizard (IFLO) Algorithm is developed
and proposed to solve the optimal planning problem (OPP) of
RESs within the radial distribution grids (RDGs).
2. A more realistic approach based on Beta and Weibull probability
density functions (PDFs) is operated to model the stochastic
behavior of PV and WT power generation, respectively, based
on real historical data collected over a decade from the study
area.
3. The optimal locations and number of WTs and PV strings, as
well as the PF of WTs, are determined simultaneously under sea-
sonal uncertainties. This aims to reduce average annual power
losses and voltage deviation (VD) while enhancing the yearly
average voltage stability index (VSI), through a multi-objective
optimization problem formulation.

The subsequent parts of the paper are organized as follows: Sec-
tion 2 introduces the probabilistic system parameters model, which
includes both load and RESs. Section 3 provides a detailed mathemat-
ical formulation of the objective functions and constraints. The design
of the FLO and the proposed IFLO algorithms is described in Sections
4 and 5, respectively. The analysis of load profiles and weather data
is discussed in Section 6. Section 7 presents the simulation results and
discussion. Finally, Section 8 concludes the paper and outlines future
research directions.
2. System modeling
This section details the modeling approaches for each uncertain pa-
rameter. The study considers time-varying constant load demand. Since
power generated by WTs and solar PV systems depends on meteorologi-
cal factors like wind speed, solar irradiance, and ambient temperature,
the stochastic behavior of these factors must be thoroughly analyzed
during the initial phase to ensure efficient integration of WT and PV
systems.
2.1. Load modeling
The system being studied is presumed to adhere to the time-varying
load curve of the IEEE-RTS [34,35]. To analyze seasonal variations
in demand, the yearly load is segmented into four seasons: summer,
autumn, winter, and spring. Each load season is represented by the
hourly load of each day (24 h). Thus, with four season days, this results
in 96 h (24 × 4), representing the entire year load (8760 h).

3. Problem articulation
The problem presented in this paper is to address the challenge
of optimizing the locations and sizes of RESs (WTs and solar PV),
alongside the PF of WT, within the RDG. The goal is to achieve optimal
grid operation through both separate and simultaneous optimizations.
The detailed mathematical formulations of the three objective functions
and constraints are presented in the next subsections.
3.1. Objective functions
The main goal of this optimization problem is to reduce power losses
and the voltage deviation, while improve the voltage stability index
while adhering to various equality and inequality constraints.

6. Data analysis
Analyzing weather data at the specified location, along with load

distribution grid. The system being studied adheres to the time-varying
load curve of the IEEE-RTS system [34,35]. Accordingly, the seasonal
hourly load profile is presented in Fig. 5 as a percentage of the annual
peak load.
Historical data on wind speed, solar irradiance, and ambient tem-
perature was collected from In Salah region, a province located in
central Algeria, in the Sahara, over a decade (from 01 January 2012 to
31 December 2021). The data are available on the NASA website [49].
Fig. 6 shows the precise location of In Salah Province. Each year within
this study period is divided into four seasons: summer (May to July),
autumn (August to October), winter (November to January), and spring
(February to April). Each season is represented by a single day of

8. Conclusion
This research addressed the complex challenge of the optimal plan-
ning problem of RESs, specifically WT and PV farms within the dis-
tribution grids. Our primary goal was to enhance system performance
by minimizing power losses and voltage deviations while improving
the voltage stability index, across the entire system. We proposed a
novel improved FLO algorithm (IFLO) specifically designed to solve
the presented problem. The IFLO incorporates three distinct strategies,
including FDB, QOBL and CM to enhance its searching capabilities
and avoid it getting trapped in local optima. We tested the IFLO on
23 different functions and compared it to other effective optimization
algorithms, such as GWO, HHO, CDO, DOA, WOA, BKA, and the
original FLO. The results show that IFLO achieves superior performance
compared to conventional algorithms. The optimal locations and rating
capacities of PV strings and WTs, along with the optimal PF of WTs,
were determined simultaneously. The planning process accounted for
seasonal uncertainties in wind speed, solar irradiance, and temperature
throughout the year, alongside the seasonal fluctuation in load demand,
all within a time-dependent generation-load model. The proposed ap-
proach effectively solved the OPP of RESs into the 85-bus distribution
grid, reducing power losses, elevating the voltage profile, and improv-
ing grid voltage stability. Specifically, IFLO reduces annual average
power losses by 70.25%, decreases voltage deviation by 78.51%, and
enhances the voltage stability index by 20.79% compared to the base
case, outperforming other recent optimization techniques such as GWO,
BKA and the original FLO. These results highlight the effectiveness
and robustness of the proposed method in addressing the complex
challenges of RES planning within the distribution grid, making it
a valuable and efficient tool for future applications in modern grid
planning. Future research could explore more complex integrations,
such as electric vehicle (EV) charging stations alongside RESs in larger
distribution grids. We aim to expand the current framework by incorpo-
